introduction.intro: The starting point for the booklet: practical principles for responding calmly to confusing or unpleasant experiences.
questions: How can I respond when an interaction leaves me feeling unsettled?
What should I do before drawing conclusions about unusual behaviour?

record_ignore_report.intro: A practical guide to recording what happened without getting drawn into provocation, setting it aside until calm, seeking health support and reporting concerns factually.
questions: What is a manageable way to record troubling remarks without letting them dominate my day?
When and how should I share concerns with my GP, a mental health professional or the police?

never_engage.intro: Why provocative remarks are tempting to answer, how debate can prolong an unwanted interaction, and ways to disengage without losing time or sleep.
questions: Why do I feel compelled to respond to an insulting or obviously false remark?
How do conversational reciprocity and turn-taking make it harder to ignore a provocation?

the_only_way_to_win_is_not_to_play.intro: Why good-faith disagreements may respond to communication while deliberate psychological manipulation can use further engagement to continue the interaction; advice to disengage rather than argue.
questions: What is the difference between good-faith conflict and deliberate psychological manipulation?
Why might arguing or explaining yourself keep an unwanted interaction going?

up_or_down.intro: A simple way to stop dwelling on repeated upsetting statements: label their apparent emotional pull as Up or Down, then move on without debating the words.
questions: How can I resist the urge to analyse or answer every repeated remark?
What do the Up and Down labels mean when I want to disengage?

ready_to_report.intro: A practical guide to documenting troubling experiences, discussing them with your GP and reporting concerns to the police calmly and factually.
questions: How should I document upsetting experiences and distinguish facts from interpretations?
How can I seek GP support and report concerns to the police in a clear, proportionate way?

take_back_control.intro: A discussion of how to make ordinary decisions on your own terms when someone else's behaviour feels intrusive or demanding.
questions: How can I regain a sense of control without confronting anyone?
Why is it helpful to stick to ordinary plans and routines?

dont_chase.intro: Explores the value of not pursuing provocations or trying to catch someone in the act.
questions: Why can chasing a suspected provocation make a situation worse?
What can I do instead of investigating every upsetting incident?

dont_tolerate_mistreatment.intro: Advice about setting boundaries, recording what happened and reporting concerns without unnecessary confrontation.
questions: How can I address mistreatment without escalating a conflict?
When should I document a problem or use a formal complaint route?

sleep_discipline.intro: Practical suggestions for protecting sleep, reducing interruptions and making stressful days more manageable.
questions: How can I reduce day-to-day stress without becoming preoccupied with it?
What sleep habits may help when I am dealing with unpleasant experiences?

drugs_and_alcohol.intro: Practical advice about alcohol and drug use during stressful situations, including dependence, impaired judgement, seeking medical advice before withdrawal and where to find support.
questions: How can I reduce the risks associated with drinking alcohol or taking drugs when under psychological pressure?
Where can I get professional help with alcohol or drug dependence, including advice about stopping safely?

feelings_can_change.intro: Practical advice on checking assumptions, assessing evidence and remembering that distressing emotional reactions can change over time.
questions: How can I distinguish what happened from an assumption about it?
Why can emotions change, and when should I seek professional support?

its_fine_to_change_your_mind.intro: Why people want to remain consistent, and why it is reasonable to reconsider an agreement made under pressure when you can decide freely.
questions: Why can it feel difficult to change my mind after I have agreed to something?
Is it reasonable to reconsider an agreement made when I felt pressured or frightened?

stay_grounded.intro: Practical advice for checking assumptions, considering simpler explanations, and separating direct experience from interpretation.
questions: How can I stay grounded when an unusual experience prompts increasingly elaborate theories?
How can I distinguish what I observed from an explanation I am considering?

personal_security_notes.intro: Everyday personal-security considerations and ways to reduce avoidable exposure to problems.
questions: Which practical security habits are worth adopting?
How can I improve personal security without constant checking?

phone_calls.intro: Considerations for unexpected telephone calls, caller identity and choosing whether to engage.
questions: How can I handle an unsolicited or unsettling phone call?
How much can I rely on the displayed telephone number or apparent voice?

social_media.intro: Looks at social-media boundaries and ways to reduce distraction, unwanted contact and exposure.
questions: How can I use social media without inviting unnecessary conflict?
When does muting, blocking or limiting notifications make sense?

how_to_collaborate.intro: A guide to sharing carefully anonymised accounts and suggesting improvements to the open booklet.
questions: How can I contribute an experience without identifying myself or others?
What should I review before sending a public contribution?

gaslit_by_friends.intro: Discusses friendship patterns that may undermine confidence, trust and personal boundaries.
questions: What behaviours might suggest an unhealthy pattern in a friendship?
How can I respond if a friend repeatedly dismisses my recollections or boundaries?

obstruction_of_communication.intro: Explains how unjustified interference with calls, messages or correspondence can isolate someone from independent support, and how to respond proportionately.
questions: When does a restriction on communication become unreasonable or coercive?
How can I seek independent advice if a call or message is being obstructed?

negging_psychological_manipulation.intro: Explains belittling remarks and backhanded compliments as forms of social pressure.
questions: What is negging and how might it appear in ordinary conversation?
How can I respond to repeated put-downs without arguing about intent?

good_cop_bad_cop.intro: Describes a contrasting-reactions tactic in which warmth and pressure may be alternated.
questions: What is the good cop, bad cop technique?
How can alternating kindness and pressure affect a person's decisions?

stockholm_syndrome.intro: Explains the debated term Stockholm syndrome, how appeasement or attachment may arise under coercion, and how to support independent decisions without blaming survivors.
questions: Why might someone appear loyal or grateful towards a person who has frightened or controlled them?
What is the difference between a safety response and freely choosing or approving of mistreatment?

guilt_tripping.intro: Explores attempts to use guilt to influence decisions or make ordinary boundaries feel unreasonable.
questions: How can I recognise guilt-based pressure?
How can I decline an unreasonable request without debating my character?

accusations_of_disloyalty.intro: Explains how ordinary decisions and harmless remarks may be framed as betrayal, creating artificial loyalty tests and guilt.
questions: Why might an innocuous action be described as turning against someone?
How can I respond calmly to an unsupported accusation of disloyalty?

emotional_burden_trick.intro: Considers situations in which one person is made to feel responsible for another person's feelings or choices.
questions: When is someone asking me to take responsibility for their emotions?
How can I show concern while keeping healthy boundaries?

accusation_baiting.intro: Discusses how a provocative accusation can divert attention from the original issue.
questions: How can an accusation pull a conversation away from the facts?
What is a calm way to respond to an unsupported allegation?

accusation_laundering.intro: Explains how repeating an unverified allegation as fact can make it seem accepted, without adding evidence or independent corroboration.
questions: Why might an accusation sound more credible when someone recounts it as though it were already true?
How can repetition and retelling make one person's allegation seem independently corroborated?

staged_third_party_reactions.intro: Explores how an apparently spontaneous third-party reaction can invite shame or speculation when the subject of the remark is unclear.
questions: Why might a seemingly independent reaction seem more convincing than a direct insult?
How can I avoid filling in the missing context of an ambiguous remark?

fake_shock.intro: Explores how apparent shock or sympathy may influence trust and decisions about reporting, while distinguishing genuine concern from possible performance.
questions: How might apparent shock encourage trust or discourage someone from reporting a concern?
Why is an emotional reaction alone insufficient to establish a speaker's intentions?

induced_sympathy.intro: How a convincingly despondent tone can invite sympathy, guilt or reassurance even when the words contain no request, and how to keep appropriate boundaries.
questions: Can a distressed-sounding voice encourage sympathy without an explicit request?
How can I maintain boundaries while taking genuine requests for help seriously?

we_only_do_this_to_really_bad_people.intro: Explains how claiming that harsh treatment is reserved for 'really bad people' can imply guilt without evidence, justify cruelty and discourage seeking help.
questions: Why does being told that mistreatment is reserved for bad people not establish guilt?
How can I respond to vague accusations without accepting their premise?

manufactured_moral_justification.intro: Describes a possible tactic where conspicuous outrage about alleged past wrongdoing invites people to treat current mistreatment as deserved, without showing a valid connection.
questions: Why doesn't an allegation about someone's past automatically justify how they are treated now?
How can loud moral condemnation imply guilt or social agreement without proving either?
When is an overheard conversation too ambiguous to infer deliberate manipulation?

claim_inflation.intro: Explores how the seriousness or scope of an accusation may change as it is repeated.
questions: What happens when an allegation becomes more dramatic over time?
How can I keep track of the original statement rather than later embellishments?

claiming_influence.intro: Examines claims of influence over other people's actions or organisations, including taking credit for ordinary events and threatening to relay casual comments.
questions: How can I assess a claim that someone caused another person's ordinary behaviour?
Why should I avoid assuming that an offhand opinion has been passed on to a third party?

claiming_control_over_predictable_events.intro: Explains how knowing the timing of an automatic or regularly scheduled event can be mistaken for having caused it.
questions: How can a person appear to control an event simply by knowing its schedule?
What routine explanations should I consider for an accurately timed prediction?

reputation_to_live_up_to.intro: Explains how assigning someone a flattering identity can influence behaviour, and how exaggerated praise may encourage unrealistic beliefs about their abilities.
questions: How can flattering descriptions be used to pressure someone into a decision?
What is the difference between encouragement and exaggerated claims about someone's abilities?

outcome_inflation_deflation.intro: Explores how sweeping predictions of success or failure can distort motivation, decisions and satisfaction, and how to assess them using evidence rather than hype or dismissal.
questions: How can exaggerated predictions of success or failure influence someone's decisions?
How do I judge a project fairly when other people make extreme predictions about it?

ego_inflation_deflation.intro: Explains how remarks implying exceptional importance or unwarranted arrogance can affect self-image, and why neither should drive decisions without evidence.
questions: How can an apparently admiring remark encourage overconfidence without offering explicit praise?
How can a dismissive remark challenge someone's self-image and invite them to prove themselves?

temptation_to_win.intro: Explains why obviously weak insults and arguments can invite unwanted debate, how criticism followed by flattery can prolong engagement, and why recording briefly then disengaging may help.
questions: Why can an easily disproved insult feel especially tempting to argue against?
How can a shift from criticism to exaggerated praise keep someone involved in an unwanted exchange?

manufactured_confusion.intro: Explains how contradictory instructions, shifting explanations and changing rules can create confusion and dependence on repeated clarification.
questions: How can I distinguish deliberate confusion from an ordinary misunderstanding?
How can I respond when instructions keep changing or no stable answer is given?

logic_traps.intro: Explains false dilemmas, circular reasoning and double binds, with suggestions for rejecting unsupported premises.
questions: How can I recognise a false dilemma or circular argument?
What can I say when every response is framed as wrong?

weaponised_literalism.intro: Explains how an argument can be derailed through excessively literal interpretations of everyday language, and how to return to the underlying point.
questions: How can strict definitions of ordinary words derail a conversation?
How do I distinguish genuine clarification from semantic nitpicking?

loaded_questions.intro: Looks at questions and conditional promises that appear to assume wrongdoing before any facts have been established.
questions: What makes a question loaded with an unproven assumption?
How can I respond without accepting an implied confession?

false_assistance.intro: Discusses instances in which controlling behaviour is presented as help or concern, particularly when relief is promised in exchange for compliance.
questions: How can a claim of concern be used to justify unreasonable demands?
What distinguishes genuine assistance from coercive conditions?

using_concern_as_a_vehicle_for_intimidat.intro: Explains how claims of concern or protection can be used to justify intimidating restrictions or demands, and how to evaluate those demands on their merits.
questions: How can I distinguish necessary safeguarding or healthcare boundaries from coercive demands framed as care?
How can I acknowledge someone's concern without agreeing to an unnecessary or humiliating demand?

you_can_run_but_you_cant_hide.intro: Explores the false choice between fleeing and hiding, and challenges claims that ordinary lawful decisions automatically imply guilt.
questions: Why does leaving or staying not establish guilt?
How can I make ordinary decisions without following an intimidator's rules?

false_endings.intro: Looks at promises or suggestions that an unpleasant situation has ended when that outcome is uncertain.
questions: Why might repeated promises of closure affect someone?
How can I avoid making decisions based on an unconfirmed ending?

false_completion.intro: Discusses the appearance that a process or demand has been satisfied when no meaningful resolution has occurred.
questions: How can I tell whether a matter has actually been resolved?
Why are clear written outcomes more useful than vague reassurance?

impossible_compliance.intro: Examines demands framed in ways that make successful compliance difficult or undefined.
questions: What does an impossible demand look like?
How can I respond when the rules seem to change whenever I comply?

impossible_standards.intro: Explores repeated criticism based on standards that are inconsistent or unattainable.
questions: How do unreasonable standards affect confidence and decision-making?
What is the difference between constructive feedback and constant fault-finding?

attacking_your_priorities.intro: Explores criticism that concedes someone's words were correct but treats their order as proof of faulty priorities, and explains why the wider inference may not follow.
questions: Does saying correct things in the wrong order necessarily reveal someone's underlying priorities?
How can I recognise when a practical comment about emphasis becomes an unsupported judgement about character?

moral_accusations.intro: Examines the use of sweeping moral accusations to pressure someone or derail a discussion.
questions: Why can a morally loaded accusation be difficult to answer?
How can I focus on specific actions rather than an exaggerated label?

moral_blackmail.intro: Discusses appeals to a supposedly greater good as a way of discouraging legitimate questions or complaints.
questions: What is moral blackmail?
How can I assess a request to stay silent for a claimed greater good?

interpretation_trick.intro: Explores how ordinary words or behaviour can be given an unexpectedly negative interpretation.
questions: How might an innocent action be framed as evidence of something else?
How can I distinguish observation from someone else's interpretation?

retrospective_reinterpretation_of_behavi.intro: Examines how ordinary actions can be assigned condemnatory meanings after the fact, particularly when accusations and standards change in response to reasonable explanations.
questions: How can I distinguish a genuine misunderstanding from repeated retroactive accusations?
What should I do when someone assigns hidden intentions to ordinary behaviour without identifying a clear rule or harm?

talking.intro: Discusses possible ambiguities in indirect communication and the temptation to infer hidden messages.
questions: How can I avoid overinterpreting an ambiguous remark?
What is the difference between a direct statement and an inferred message?

service_shield.intro: Examines appeals to professional roles or public-service status as a defence against criticism.
questions: Does a person's professional role settle whether their conduct was appropriate?
How can I raise concerns about conduct without assuming motives?

the_guity_always_run.intro: Explores the flawed idea that avoiding confrontation automatically indicates guilt.
questions: Does leaving a tense situation imply guilt?
Why might disengaging be a reasonable response to provocation?

legal_intimidation.intro: Looks at threatening references to courts or legal consequences and the value of checking formal information.
questions: How can I respond to an intimidating legal claim?
When is independent legal guidance more useful than arguing?

hiding_behind_OSA.intro: Examines claims of official secrecy or classified authority used to deter questions or reporting, and the importance of checking the actual law.
questions: Does invoking the Official Secrets Act automatically prohibit reporting concerns?
How can I describe what was said without speculating about any alleged technology?

criminilisation.intro: Discusses framing ordinary actions as wrongdoing without a clear factual or legal basis.
questions: How can everyday behaviour be unfairly described as criminal?
What should I check before accepting somebody's legal interpretation?

threatened_framing.intro: Examines threats that someone will fabricate accusations or arrange misleading appearances.
questions: What can I do if someone threatens to make a false accusation?
How can I document a threat without confronting the person making it?

accidentally_overheard.intro: Discusses remarks that appear to have been overheard and why their context may be unclear.
questions: How reliable is a fragment of conversation overheard by chance?
How can I avoid reacting to remarks that may not concern me?

narrating_trick.intro: Looks at unsolicited descriptions of someone else's actions and the effect of repeated commentary.
questions: Why might persistent commentary feel intrusive?
How can I decide whether a remark requires any response?

public_shaming.intro: Discusses public embarrassment, social pressure and non-confrontational ways to protect boundaries.
questions: What is public shaming and how does it affect behaviour?
How can I respond when I feel embarrassed or singled out in public?

name_and_shame.intro: Examines the social consequences of labelling or publicly identifying someone in a disparaging way.
questions: What distinguishes legitimate criticism from public humiliation?
What should I do if a damaging label is repeated about someone?

flashmobs.intro: Explores how coordinated-looking group behaviour can influence perception and reactions.
questions: Why can group behaviour feel more convincing than an individual remark?
How can I avoid drawing conclusions about strangers' intentions from a crowd?

body_shaming.intro: Discusses remarks that criticise someone's appearance or private bodily characteristics.
questions: How can I handle insulting comments about my body?
When is it appropriate to disengage from body-related criticism?

exaggerated_disgust.intro: Explains how frequent, theatrical expressions of disgust about minor or alleged faults can create shame and excessive self-monitoring, and how to respond proportionately.
questions: Why can repeated expressions of disgust make a small criticism feel overwhelming?
How should I respond to an exaggerated hygiene-related criticism or an ambiguous overheard remark?

humiliation_rituals.intro: Describes coercive demands to perform or endure degrading acts as conditions of acceptance or assistance, and how to protect dignity and set boundaries.
questions: How can I distinguish a necessary uncomfortable request from an unnecessary humiliation ritual?
What is a safe, proportionate response to a degrading demand from someone in authority?

bodily_functions.intro: Explores the embarrassment that can arise when ordinary bodily functions are treated as shameful or suspicious.
questions: Are ordinary bodily functions a reasonable basis for moral accusations?
How can I maintain boundaries around private bodily matters?

incitement_to_violence.intro: Discusses provocative behaviour and the importance of avoiding retaliatory violence.
questions: How can I respond when someone appears to be trying to provoke a fight?
Why is walking away safer than trying to win a confrontation?

cumulative_psychological_pressure.intro: Explains how repeated stressful experiences can accumulate into exhaustion and vigilance even when they have different causes, with practical ways to recover attention.
questions: How can repeated minor disruptions affect sleep, concentration and everyday functioning?
What can I do to reduce cumulative stress without analysing every unclear incident?

sleep_deprivation.intro: Examines how inadequate sleep can affect attention, judgement and responses to stressful interactions.
questions: How might poor sleep affect my interpretation of upsetting events?
What practical steps can help protect sleep during stressful periods?

sleep_deprivation_reinforcement.intro: A proposed interaction between sleep loss, susceptibility to misleading information and repetition that could make an interpretation feel convincing after sleep improves.
questions: Could repeated misleading statements feel more credible when someone is sleep-deprived?
Can a familiar interpretation persist after sleep recovers, and what does research actually show?

deprivation_of_basic_necessities.intro: Describes the coercive withholding of essential needs such as food, water, hygiene, rest and medical attention, while distinguishing punitive restrictions from legitimate care constraints.
questions: How can I distinguish a genuine care or safety restriction from punitive withholding of an essential need?
What practical steps can I take if I am denied food, water, hygiene or necessary medical care?

sexual_coercion.intro: Discusses threats, humiliation and violations of sexual boundaries in a non-graphic context.
questions: What forms can sexual coercion or sexual blackmail take?
Where can someone seek help after threats involving intimate information?

choose_your_death.intro: Considers threats and coercive ultimatums involving harm, and the importance of safety over engagement.
questions: How should I treat a threat involving serious harm?
Why is it important to seek safety rather than negotiate a threatening ultimatum?

indefinite_abuse.intro: Explores the distress caused by claims that an unpleasant situation will never end.
questions: How can I respond to a statement that a bad situation is permanent?
What can I focus on when someone makes an open-ended threat?

threatening_consequences_for_seeking_hel.intro: Describes intimidation designed to discourage someone from seeking help, including threatened retaliation for reporting concerns or contacting independent advisers.
questions: How can I distinguish an honest warning about a complaint's practical consequences from a coercive threat?
Where can I obtain independent advice about reporting safely if someone is threatening retaliation?

preemptive_discrediting.intro: Explains how remarks such as 'Nobody will believe him' or claims about large amounts of unseen evidence can undermine confidence in being heard, without establishing what others think or whether the supposed evidence exists.
questions: Why might a prediction of disbelief or a claim about undisclosed evidence discourage someone from seeking help?
How can I respond without assuming an ambiguous remark was intended for me or treating an unsupported claim as fact?

dream_manipulation.intro: Explains how sounds incorporated into dreams, cold reading and post-waking suggestibility can create the impression that dreams are being influenced or observed, without establishing dream control.
questions: Can spoken sounds heard during sleep influence dream content?
How might cold reading or suggestibility after waking make someone seem to know what I dreamed?

cold_reading.intro: Introduces cold reading and the role of broad statements, observation and selective feedback.
questions: How can a plausible guess appear surprisingly personal?
What is the difference between cold reading and genuinely knowing private information?

cold_reading_ai_assisted.intro: Explores hypothetical uses of AI for personalised predictions and their technical limitations.
questions: How might AI make cold reading seem more convincing?
What are the limits of predicting someone's thoughts from contextual information?

predicting_bodily_movements.intro: Explores how a remark apparently anticipating an ordinary movement can be paired with an accusation, and offers practical advice about disengagement and webcam privacy.
questions: Can subtle movement cues help predict a person's next movement?
How can I respond to a disturbing remark that seems timed to an ordinary movement?

source_identification_trick.intro: Discusses how suggestions about who a statement concerns can influence interpretation and memory.
questions: How might a person infer who a vague remark refers to?
Why does a confident guess not necessarily establish knowledge of private thoughts?

internal_monologue_trick.intro: Explores source confusion and suggestions about the origin of thoughts or speech.
questions: How might suggestion affect the way a statement is attributed?
What are source-monitoring errors and how should they be interpreted cautiously?

inner_voice_technique.intro: Explores a proposed, unproven acoustic mechanism combining ear-specific HRTF knowledge and MRI-derived vocal-tract modelling to examine whether recorded speech could seem less external.
questions: Could personalised vocal-tract filtering change how a recorded voice resembles one's self-voice?
Why does bone conduction matter when hearing your own voice?
Can a single distant loudspeaker reduce external localisation cues by filtering alone?

mind_reading_trick.intro: Examines how apparently accurate observations may create an impression of mind reading.
questions: Why can a good prediction feel like someone knows what I am thinking?
What information can and cannot be inferred from observable behaviour?

bug_in_face.intro: Discusses speculative ways observable facial cues might be used to infer feelings or topics.
questions: What can facial expressions reveal about someone's emotional state?
What are the limits of interpreting a person's thoughts from their face?

manipulated_media.intro: Explores altered images, recordings and other media alongside practical verification questions.
questions: How can a digital recording be edited or presented misleadingly?
What checks are sensible before relying on online media?

pwned-devices.intro: Examines the consequences of compromised devices and sensible ways to verify digital information.
questions: What could a compromised device allow an attacker to change or see?
What practical checks are useful if I suspect a security issue?

air_gap_limitations.intro: Explores what separating a device from a network does and does not protect against.
questions: What is an air gap in computer security?
Why does keeping a device offline not address every security risk?

there_is_no_privacy.intro: Discusses the limits of digital privacy and the choices people can still make about personal data.
questions: What aspects of everyday digital activity may expose personal information?
How can I improve privacy without trying to eliminate every possible risk?

streisand-effect.intro: Describes how attempts to suppress information can attract attention, without encouraging confrontation or deliberate provocation.
questions: What is the Streisand effect?
Why is it better to document and report concerns calmly than to provoke a reaction?

conclusion.intro: Closing reflections on maintaining boundaries and making practical decisions in difficult circumstances.
questions: What are the most useful principles to remember?
How can I move forward without staying engaged with unpleasant experiences?

victim_blaming.intro: Examines how blame can be redirected onto someone who reports mistreatment, and ways to stay focused on conduct rather than labels.
questions: What is victim blaming and role reversal?
How can I stay focused on facts when labels are disputed?

dont_do_it_yourself.intro: Discusses the importance of avoiding self-harm, retaliation or irreversible decisions in response to perceived provocation.
questions: How can I avoid acting impulsively in response to pressure?
What safer options can I choose when a situation feels overwhelming?

false_report_accusations.intro: Explores accusations that someone has filed a false report, how such claims may discourage legitimate complaints, and ways to respond calmly and factually.
questions: What is the difference between an unsubstantiated report and a deliberately false one?
How can I respond to an accusation of false reporting without abandoning a genuine concern?

fabricated_confession.intro: Examines a claim that someone has just confessed to a crime, the difference between an accusation and an actual admission, and how to avoid reacting to an unsupported assertion.
questions: Why does 'He just said ...' sound like evidence when it may be only an allegation?
When is a false attribution better described as gaslighting, and how can I record the facts without reacting?

how_to_fork.intro: A beginner-friendly guide to forking this website, personalising its content and design, and publishing your own version for free with optional ChatGPT guidance.
questions: How can I fork and republish this website with GitHub Pages?
Can ChatGPT guide me through creating and maintaining a personal version without coding?

how_to_record.intro: Practical steps for keeping dated, factual notes of comments and incidents, preserving available evidence and managing correspondence by email.
questions: What should I include when I email myself a record of something I heard or observed?
How can I keep evidence and correspondence organised for later review?

the_time_gap.intro: Advice on setting troubling interactions aside, avoiding real-time searches or analysis in response, and deciding independently when something needs attention.
questions: Why can reacting or searching in real time make an upsetting interaction harder to set aside?
How can I make decisions on my own schedule while still acting promptly when safety is at risk?

listening_in.intro: Why listening out for personally relevant fragments can reinforce hypervigilance, and why ignoring overheard conversations protects attention.
questions: Why does hearing my name make a background conversation difficult to ignore?
Why is it better not to try to interpret conversations I can only partly hear?

primed_thought_attribution.intro: A hypothetical sequence in which hearing a phrase makes it mentally accessible before someone claims the listener just thought it. Explains priming, source monitoring and why apparent thought-reading does not follow.
questions: How can hearing a phrase make it come to mind shortly afterwards?
Why does recognising a thought not prove someone knows what I was thinking?

thought_attribution_suggestion_repetitio.intro: A research-grounded hypothesis about falsely attributing a recently heard phrase to someone's thoughts, and whether repetition during poor sleep could make the feeling persist.
questions: How might an accusation change someone's judgment about where a familiar phrase came from?
What research supports source-monitoring errors, repetition and sleep deprivation, and what remains untested?

prediction_priming_feedback.intro: A hypothesis combining personalised prediction, priming, source misattribution and multimodal sensor fusion, including weak acoustic cues such as hesitation and humming, to explain apparent thought-reading and reaction feedback.
questions: How might spoken predictions and priming change the listener's subsequent associations?
What could microphones, cameras, Wi-Fi sensing or mmWave radar observe during a reaction?
Why can observable feedback increase a model's confidence without proving a prediction of private thoughts was correct?

continuous_behavioural_prediction.intro: A hypothetical use of a continuously updated LLM to predict an individual's likely next actions from behavioural history, then combine those estimates with other observations.
questions: How could an LLM use a chronological history of someone's actions to estimate what they may do next?
Why might low-confidence behavioural predictions still provide useful context alongside other measurements?

priming_ambiguous_accusations.intro: A proposed sequence in which a phrase primes an idea, a later ambiguous accusation invites the listener to supply a referent, and unsuccessful attempts may still act as repetition or provocation.
questions: Does the priming voice have to sound like my own?
How can an ambiguous accusation seem personal without identifying anybody?
What if none of the attempts has an effect?

habituation_and_recovery.intro: The hopeful possibility that repeated provocations can lose emotional impact, how responses can return after a break, and why no fixed reset period can be inferred.
questions: Why might a repeated insult eventually have less impact?
Can habituation return after a fortnight or a month?
Why is non-engagement preferable to analysing each remark?

quiet_speech_masking_attention.intro: Why someone listening for a quiet, familiar voice might notice speech that others miss under instrumental music or background noise, and how stress and expectation can also create false detections.
questions: Can a quiet familiar voice be noticed when other people are not paying attention?
How do instrumental music, a sleep noise machine and selective attention affect speech detection?
Can prolonged stress and expectation make someone hear speech in ambiguous background audio?

suggested_mishearings.intro: A hypothetical use of AI-generated similar-sounding words to suggest what somebody supposedly heard. Explains perceptual priming, post-event suggestion, and why a plausible guess is not knowledge of another person's private perception.
questions: Why can two similar-sounding words be confused when speech is unclear?
Can suggesting a different word affect what I subsequently remember hearing?
Does an accurate guess about what I heard demonstrate access to my thoughts?

cross_conversation_sentence_assembly.intro: Explores how priming might make fragments of different conversations seem to form a personally meaningful sentence, and how monitoring for more fragments could lead to persistent hypervigilance.
questions: Why might a combination of separate conversations feel meaningful to one listener but not to others?
How can searching for hidden sentences in everyday conversations reinforce hypervigilance?
Why is ignoring ambiguous remarks safer than reacting to them?

creating_the_appearance_of_guilt.intro: How persistent stress and public accusations can make someone more watchful or hesitant, and how those reactions may be misread as evidence of guilt.
questions: Why might someone become hesitant or hypervigilant after repeated stressful encounters?
Why is nervous or unusual public behaviour not evidence of wrongdoing?

pretend_planning.intro: Explains how indistinct, seemingly purposeful speech might draw someone's attention away from another activity; includes everyday descriptions of the pattern and reassurance when an indistinct conversation is their only concern.
questions: Why might a barely audible conversation distract me from what I am doing?
If all I have noticed is an indistinct conversation next door, do I need to do anything?

the_imaginary_line.intro: Explains how a vague declaration that someone has crossed a boundary can create apprehension about unspecified consequences, and why an ambiguous remark need not prompt an immediate response.
questions: What makes phrases such as 'Right, that's it!' or 'Now you're for it' feel threatening when no consequence is specified?
How can I avoid getting drawn into trying to work out what an ambiguous remark means?

presence_threat.intro: Explores how a person's deliberately signalled presence can be used as an implied threat, creating fear and anticipation without an explicit confrontation.
questions: How can someone's presence be used to communicate an implied threat?
What is a practical response to an intimidating presence without engaging?

delayed_responses_from_organisations.intro: How to use delays from organisations to regain composure, organise records, make Subject Access Requests, and pursue complaints calmly and persistently.
questions: How can I make constructive use of a slow response from an organisation?
What can I do about a complaint I could not raise promptly, and when should I follow up?

spatial_audio.intro: Explains how HRTF processing can change the perceived direction of reproduced speech, including when played through car speakers.
questions: How can spatial audio make a voice seem to come from above or behind the listener?
What roles do HRTF processing, speaker placement and cabin acoustics play?
Can a connected phone supply preprocessed spatial audio to a car stereo?

fear_of_hacking.intro: Explains how constant discussion of hypothetical hacking threats can turn ordinary technology use into a source of hypervigilance and distraction, even without an actual intrusion.
questions: How can fear of hacking distract someone from what they are trying to achieve?
When does sensible cybersecurity awareness become disproportionate threat monitoring?

invoking_an_imagined_audience.intro: Explains how invoking an absent audience's predicted reaction can create social pressure and lend an unsupported judgement borrowed authority.
questions: How can references to what the press, a jury, the police or everyone supposedly thinks be used to pressure someone?
Why is a prediction about an absent audience's reaction not the same as evidence of its actual view?

downplaying_trauma.intro: Explains how minimising distressing experiences, comparing suffering or pressuring someone to move on can undermine confidence in their own response.
questions: How can someone downplay a distressing experience without denying that it happened?
Why can comparisons with other people's suffering make someone question whether their own distress is legitimate?
How can pressure to move on discourage someone from seeking support?

minimising_the_effect.intro: Explores how serious or repeated behaviour can be described as harmless teasing while the affected person's objection is made to look unreasonable.
questions: How can calling harmful conduct 'just a joke' shift attention from the conduct to a person's reaction?
Why does omitting the cumulative context make an objection seem disproportionate?
How can I distinguish a genuine apology for a bad joke from repeated dismissal of serious objections?

projection.intro: Explains how someone may attribute their own feelings, intentions or behaviour to another person, shifting attention away from the conduct at issue.
questions: What is projection in a disagreement?
How can an accusation put someone on the defensive and distract from the original behaviour?
How can I distinguish a possible projection from an ordinary disagreement?

attributing_displaced_anger.intro: Explains how a claim that someone is taking their anger out on another person can assign motives, redirect responsibility and create conflict around an unverified explanation.
questions: How can a claim about displaced anger influence who gets blamed for someone's behaviour?
Why should I distinguish someone's actions from an explanation of their motives?

implied_consequences.intro: Explains how remarks such as 'Keep digging!' can imply that continuing an unspecified action will lead to unspecified trouble, leaving the listener to supply both meanings.
questions: What makes 'Keep digging!' an example of implied consequences?
How can an ambiguous remark make ordinary actions feel risky without specifying a threat?
How is an implied consequence different from a direct threat or an unspecified boundary warning?

poisoned_encouragement.intro: Explains how apparent encouragement, predictions of harm and claims of permission can cause someone to question or abandon an otherwise independent decision.
questions: What is poisoned encouragement, and how can apparent approval discourage an action?
How does 'Why do you think we let you do it?' imply control without demonstrating it?
How does poisoned encouragement differ from a warning that simply names a concrete risk?

staged_compliments.intro: Explains how praise timed immediately before a request or persuasive message can capture attention, encourage reciprocity and make the following message more persuasive.
questions: How can a compliment make someone more receptive to a request or persuasive message?
Why might praise immediately before a suggestion create pressure to respond warmly?

intrusion_of_privacy.intro: How unsolicited comments about spending, routines and other personal choices can make someone feel monitored, even during ordinary private activities.
questions: Why can an unexpected remark about my spending or private habits leave me feeling watched?
How can intrusive comments cause hypervigilance and self-monitoring?

pretend_superpowers.intro: How repeated apparent coincidences, misleading feedback and social reactions could create a mistaken impression of extraordinary ability.
questions: Why can a series of apparent successes make an ability seem extraordinary?
How can misleading feedback and social reinforcement distort confidence in a prediction?

false_attribution_of_causality.intro: A meta-pattern about mistaken causes: an externally produced effect can appear to result from a person's own thought, action or feeling. It distinguishes observed timing from evidence of what caused an event.
questions: How can an effect created elsewhere lead someone to believe that they caused it?
Why does a repeated coincidence not, by itself, establish causality?
How does this underlying mechanism relate to apparent superpowers or claims of control?

exploitation_of_ambiguity.intro: How incomplete statements can invite a listener to supply meanings and consequences that were never explicitly stated.
questions: How can an ambiguous remark feel specific when important details are missing?
What is the difference between a statement and the meaning a listener supplies?

manufactured_corroboration.intro: How several repetitions of one claim can create the appearance of multiple independent sources of evidence.
questions: Does repeated agreement mean several independent sources have confirmed a claim?
How can an unverified allegation become treated as established fact?

induced_reactions_as_evidence.intro: How a response to provocation can be misrepresented as evidence of an unrelated accusation or character trait.
questions: Why does somebody's emotional reaction not prove the accusation made about them?
How can leaving a confrontation be unfairly portrayed as an admission of guilt?

manufactured_no_win_situations.intro: How arbitrary, contradictory or changing rules can make every possible response appear wrong.
questions: How can a choice be presented so that every answer appears to fail?
How can shifting standards turn even reasonable compliance into a supposed offence?

attention_capture_and_conditioning.intro: How repeated cues can capture attention and create expectations through reinforcement or emotionally significant associations.
questions: How can a repeated cue draw attention away from ordinary activities?
How do intermittent reinforcement and habituation affect responses to repeated messages?

manufactured_urgency.intro: How artificially imposed deadlines or exaggerated time pressure can prompt rushed decisions by discouraging reflection or verification.
questions: How can an invented deadline make a request feel more important than it is?
Why is an apparently urgent demand different from a genuine emergency or legitimate deadline?

exploiting_natural_human_responses.intro: A meta-pattern in which a predictable human instinct is activated in circumstances where the instinctive response works against the person's interests. It examines curiosity, fairness, empathy, self-defence and urgency without assuming intent from a reaction alone.
questions: When can an ordinarily useful human instinct become counterproductive?
How can a situation invite an unhelpful response without anyone directly instructing it?
How can you check whether reacting will actually serve your interests?

manufactured_agreement.intro: Explains how someone may falsely treat listening to a song or watching a programme as agreement with controversial statements made in it.
questions: Why doesn't hearing or enjoying a song imply agreement with its lyrics?
How can falsely attributing a programme's opinions to its audience provoke defensiveness or self-censorship?
